title: end-to-end system design case studies
concepts: A case study is a way to practice applying requirements, models, data ownership, failure analysis, and tradeoffs. There is no universal diagram: a strong design begins with constraints, establishes a correct baseline, follows concrete read/write paths, and evolves only when a bottleneck or requirement demands it.
Translate product requirements into observable measures and testable user journeys before choosing components.
Make state ownership, consistency, replay, and recovery explicit at every boundary.
Account for latency, throughput, tail behavior, capacity, cost, security, privacy, and operational effort as interacting constraints.
Use a simple baseline, then add a mechanism only to meet a stated requirement or measured bottleneck.
Design failure behavior and release compatibility across client, API, data, and operations rather than per component.

sourceSnapshot.authority: The HLD Handbook public system-design syllabus, with relevant standards, framework guidance, and official platform documentation for technical context.
sourceSnapshot.edition: Handbook syllabus checked 2026-11-17; concepts are version-independent unless an implementation-specific source says otherwise.

scopeExclusions: The academy teaches original explanations and worked designs for the mapped Handbook topics and the 56 listed case prompts; it does not reproduce the Handbook's article text. Topic-to-lesson depth and factual claims are tracked separately in the coverage map and factual-review ledger.
Vendor-specific service SKUs, quotas, and configuration signatures are intentionally excluded; verify those in the selected provider’s current documentation.
The inventory names are the closed reference scope for this topic; the overview teaches the mental model without listing every item.
